hints: Think about what makes a d-block element different from a true transition element, focus on the electron configuration of the ion formed, not just the atom.
walkthrough:
Separate d-block from transition**
All transition elements sit in the d-block, but not all d-block elements count as transition elements. Look at the ions they form. Scandium forms only $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ with $[\text{Ar}]$ configuration and zinc forms only $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ with $3d^{10}$, so neither has an incomplete d subshell in its stable ion.

Apply the precise definition**
You need an element that can exist as a stable ion where the d orbitals are partly filled, such as $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ with $3d^6$ or $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ with $3d^9$. That incomplete d set is what gives transition chemistry its colour, variable oxidation states and complex formation.
Final answer: A transition element is an element which forms one or more stable ions with incomplete d orbitals.

hints: Recall what a ligand does when it bonds, it donates a lone pair into an empty orbital on the metal, so consider what empty orbitals a transition metal ion can offer.
walkthrough:
Picture ligand bonding**
A complex forms when a ligand donates a lone pair into an empty orbital on the central metal ion to make a coordinate (dative covalent) bond. For this to happen the metal must have low energy empty orbitals available.

Link to the d orbitals**
Transition metal ions have vacant 3d and 4s orbitals that are close in energy and readily accessible. Ligands such as $\text{NH}_3$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can donate into these, allowing high coordination numbers like 4 or 6.
Final answer: Transition elements have vacant d orbitals that are energetically accessible to accept lone pairs from ligands to form coordinate bonds.

hints: Think about an isolated gaseous ion with no ligands around it, there is nothing to split the d orbitals, so compare their energies.
walkthrough:
Understand degenerate in this context**
Degenerate simply means equal in energy. In an isolated $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ion there is no ligand field, so all five 3d orbitals experience the same environment.

Contrast with a complex**
Once ligands approach, the d orbitals split into higher and lower sets and are no longer degenerate. But on its own, the ion has five identical energy 3d orbitals.
Final answer: Degenerate d orbitals are orbitals of the same energy.

hints: Recall the general d-orbital shape with four lobes, then think where the $d_{xy}$ lobes point relative to the x and y axes, on the axes or between them.
walkthrough:
Recall the four lobe pattern**
All d orbitals except $d_{z^2}$ look like a four leaf clover. For $3d_{xy}$, all four lobes lie flat in the xy-plane centred on the origin.

Place the lobes correctly**
The subscript xy tells you the lobes point between the x and y axes, at $45^{\circ}$ to each axis, not along them. Nothing extends along z. Sketch four equal touching lobes in the x-y cross, with x, y and z axes clearly labelled.
Final answer: Four-lobed orbital centred at the origin lying in the xy-plane with lobes between the x and y axes (no lobe on the z-axis).

hints: For step 1, identify the ions that form the brown $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$ precipitate from $\text{AgNO}_3$ and $\text{NaOH}$, remembering $\text{NaNO}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are also formed.

For step 2, think of $\text{NH}_3$ as a ligand that dissolves the oxide by forming the linear diammine complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{+}$, balance $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Build step 1 as precipitation**
Adding $\text{OH}^{-}$ to $\text{Ag}^{+}$ first gives $\text{AgOH}$ which immediately dehydrates to brown $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$. Balancing the full equation gives $$2\text{AgNO}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{O} + 2\text{NaNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The ionic form $2\text{Ag}^{+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ is also accepted.

Build step 2 as ligand substitution**
Excess $\text{NH}_3$ acts as a ligand and redissolves the precipitate to give the colourless $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{+}$ complex. Balance Ag, N, H and O: $$\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]\text{OH}$$ This shows two moles of complex per mole of oxide.

Final answer: step 1: $2\text{AgNO}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{O} + 2\text{NaNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
step 2: $\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]\text{OH}$

hints: Consider the $\text{NH}_3$ ligand on its own, the N atom has three N-H bonds plus one coordinate bond to Ag, so work out its local geometry.
Now look at the whole $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{+}$ ion with only two ligands on Ag, use electron pair repulsion around Ag to predict the N-Ag-N angle.
walkthrough:
Fix the angle at nitrogen**
In coordinated $\text{NH}_3$, nitrogen is bonded to three H atoms and to Ag, with no lone pair left. That is four bonding pairs arranged tetrahedrally, so any H-N-Ag angle is the tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$.

Fix the shape at silver**
Silver(I) with coordination number 2 has two bonding pairs and no lone pairs on Ag. They repel to be as far apart as possible, giving a linear N-Ag-N arrangement with angle $180^{\circ}$. So the complex ion shape is linear.

Final answer: shape is linear
bond angle for H-N-Ag = $109.5^{\circ}$
bond angle for N-Ag-N = $180^{\circ}$

hints: At the positive electrode $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$ gains electrons to form Ag in alkaline conditions, balance O with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and then add $\text{OH}^{-}$ and $\text{e}^{-}$.
At the negative electrode Zn is oxidised to $\text{Zn}(\text{OH})_2$ in alkali, balance the loss of electrons with $\text{OH}^{-}$ on the left.
walkthrough:
Write the reduction half equation**
The positive electrode is the cathode where reduction happens. Silver goes from +1 in $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$ to 0 in $\text{Ag}$. In alkali you cannot use $\text{H}^{+}$, so balance O with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and produce $\text{OH}^{-}$: $$\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag} + 2\text{OH}^{-}$$ Check atoms and charge: both sides have Ag2, O2, H2 and charge 2-.

Write the oxidation half equation**
The negative electrode is the anode where Zn is oxidised from 0 to +2 in $\text{Zn}(\text{OH})_2$. Supply $\text{OH}^{-}$ from the electrolyte: $$\text{Zn} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{e}^{-}$$ Adding the two half equations cancels $2\text{e}^{-}$, $2\text{OH}^{-}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ correctly to give the overall $\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{Zn} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag} + \text{Zn}(\text{OH})_2$.

Final answer: at the positive electrode: $\text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Ag} + 2\text{OH}^{-}$
at the negative electrode: $\text{Zn} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{e}^{-}$

hints: Note that dps is drawn as N-N with each N binding a different Ru, so sketch a chain where each dps bridges two Ru centres, not chelating one Ru.
Remember each Ru is octahedral with four $\text{Cl}$ ligands plus two N atoms from two different dps ligands, so show two repeat units with continuation bonds.
walkthrough:
Use dps as a bridge**
Look at Fig. 2.2, dps has two pyridine N atoms linked by S. Here each N bonds to a different $\text{Ru}^{3+}$, so dps bridges. Represent it as N-N and draw N-Ru-N links to make a long chain, with continuation bonds at each end to show the polymer continues.

Complete octahedral Ru**
Each Ru in $[\text{Ru}(dps)\text{Cl}_4]^{-}$ is 6 coordinate: four $\text{Cl}^{-}$ plus two N atoms from two separate dps ligands. Draw each Ru with four Cl around it and two N atoms (often trans) connecting to the left and right dps units. Repeating this twice gives two repeat units of the $([\text{Ru}(dps)\text{Cl}_4]^{-})_n$ chain.

Final answer: Chain of alternating Ru and dps: --- N-Ru($\text{Cl}$)4-N --- N-Ru($\text{Cl}$)4-N --- with each Ru bonded to four $\text{Cl}$ and two N (trans N atoms), each dps N bonded to a different Ru, showing two repeat units of $[\text{Ru}(dps)\text{Cl}_4]^{-}$ with continuation bonds.
